As of 121 PM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: For the rest of the week, expect similar day to day 
weather with no precipitation with daytime temperatures about 10 to 
15 degrees above normal. A blocked pattern is associated with a 
quasi-stationary ridge centered to our south near the central 
Appalachians through Friday night, which will finally retreat to the 
northeast through southern New England and into the western Atlantic 
on Saturday. This position of the ridge isn't drawing in 
particularly warm air, which will prevent us from seeing historic 
warmth; this is reflected in the ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index, which 
has been showing each day through the weekend having somewhat 
unusual, but not extreme, temperatures. The most unusual 
temperatures from a climatological perspective are favored for 
Friday morning as breezier conditions will keep us milder than 
recent nights, especially in northern New York from the western 
Adirondacks into the northern St. Lawrence Valley.

Subtle differences can be expected each day as the upper air pattern 
evolves, which ties into the aforementioned breezier period. 
Tomorrow morning southwesterly flow and relatively moist low level 
air will support a chance of another round of localized low stratus 
downwind of the eastern Great Lakes. However, the strong upper level 
ridge with anomalous heights that currently sits over the Midwest 
will migrate eastward, with its axis centered over northern New York 
and Vermont tomorrow morning before exiting to our east. Expect the 
dry air aloft over our region to lead to mainly sunny skies tomorrow 
with temperatures near or slightly warmer than today. 

The exiting ridge will open the door for a trough to quickly 
pass through the region tomorrow night. It will bring little 
moisture but a bout of stronger winds. The nocturnal timing of 
this system will limit wind impacts, but model guidance depicts 
a belt of 40-45 knots about 2 to 3 thousand feet above ground 
level. Strong surface stability should keep these winds from 
mixing, but this will be a hazard for aviators and potentially 
out on mountain ridgelines. After sunrise, this low level jet 
should quickly weaken, and while cooler air aloft moves in with 
winds becoming westerly, deeper mixing will actually counteract 
cooling temperatures aloft, and with a milder start temperatures
will peak near or above those on Thursday, especially in the 
wider valleys. 

With the high pressure area finally moving more directly overhead 
behind this trough, a cooler night Friday night will give way to 
another warm day on Saturday. Potential terrain-driven stratocumulus 
development Friday that lingers overnight could impact temperatures 
through Saturday somewhat, but otherwise mostly sunny conditions 
will enable more of the same with highs again in the mid and upper 
50s for most locations.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Our warm dry pattern will come to a halt by early next 
week as a coastal system and approaching cold front will drive our 
weather. A robust coastal low is expected to develop off the Florida 
and Georgia coast this weekend and move up the coast towards 
southern New England. Concurrently, a cold front will swing from the 
Great Lakes eastward towards the St. Lawrence on Sunday. Models 
remain split between two scenarios. The first would mean a moderate 
rainfall event for southern and eastern Vermont, and the second 
would mean a lighter rainfall event favoring northern New York and 
the international border. In either scenario, temperatures are 
expected to fall from above normal this weekend with highs in the 
50s and lower 60s to below normal by next midweek with highs only in 
the 30s and lower 40s. Lows will experience a similar drop from 
weekend 30s/mid 40s to midweek upper teens/mid 20s.

In coastal storm Scenario 1, which the GFS deterministic model is 
currently favoring, the low hugs the east coast, phasing with the 
cold front on Monday, bringing moderate rain to southern and eastern 
Vermont. A sharp precipitation gradient would likely occur with 
drier air limiting the northward extend of the precipitation. 
Ensembles are showing 20-50% chance of a half inch of precipitation 
for southern and eastern Vermont. The latest GFS ensemble run in 
particular has shown an increase in this probability from the 
previous runs. In Scenario 2, which the ECMWF deterministic model 
currently favors, the coastal low tracks more out to sea with little 
to no impact to our region. The only precipitation would be coming 
from the weaker cold front. Precipitation on Monday would be focused 
more over northern New York and areas near the international border, 
with perhaps some isolated snow showers in the higher terrain of the 
Adirondacks and Northeast Kingdom Monday night into Tuesday.
